headline: Australia pushes tech giants to let users switch off social media algorithms
meta_description: Australia's government plans legislation allowing users to disable social media algorithms, with hefty penalties for tech firms that refuse.
summary_short: Australians could soon choose whether algorithms feed their social media content, as the government introduces digital duty of care laws this week.
body:
Australia is moving to hand users real control over their social media experience. Communications Minister Anika Wells has announced draft legislation that would allow Australians to switch off algorithmic feeds on platforms like Meta, Google, and TikTok. If tech companies refuse to offer this choice, they face substantial penalties under the new digital duty of care laws. Wells framed the move as holding a largely unregulated industry accountable: "Big tech is not a protected species and they should offer their customers basic safety standards." The legislation, expected to be introduced within days, represents Australia's latest effort to reshape how social media operates—following last year's world-first ban on social media for under-16s.

Wells acknowledged that while many Australians value algorithms for discovering local businesses and tailored content, the choice itself matters most. "We want to give Australians more choice over what they see on their social media feeds," she told the ABC. The government is still consulting experts on whether users should opt in or opt out of algorithms—a decision that could fundamentally change how the rules function in practice. Beyond algorithms, the draft laws will also require platforms to remove harmful content, including illegal pornography and material promoting disordered eating.

Not everyone backs the proposal. Opposition leader Angus Taylor expressed skepticism, fearing it amounts to censorship and arguing the government should first strengthen enforcement of the existing social media ban. However, Wells pushed back firmly, clarifying that identifying and mitigating risks on platforms is about safety, not speech suppression. Consent advocate Chanel Contos has called for an even stricter opt-in model, arguing that algorithms actively fuel harmful content including misogynistic material targeting young people. Her advocacy highlights what the legislation aims to address: the gap between user choice and corporate control.
quick_facts: Communications Minister Anika Wells leading draft legislation this week
Meta, Google, TikTok face substantial penalties for refusing algorithm controls
Builds on Australia's world-first social media ban for under-16s
Laws also target illegal pornography and disordered eating content
Government consulting experts on opt-in versus opt-out mechanisms
